name: New Orleans, LA
intro: A walkable, food- and music-driven city trip. Most first visits center on the French Quarter, with day trips out to the Garden District and Warehouse District museums.
bestTimeToVisit: October through early April is the sweet spot — mild temperatures, lower humidity, and thinner crowds outside of festival weekends. Spring (especially around Mardi Gras and Jazz Fest) is the most crowded and highest-priced stretch. Hurricane season runs June–November, with August and September the most volatile — build flexibility into trips booked in that window.
avgTripCost: Mid-range travelers commonly spend $120–$270 per person per day (3-star hotel, sit-down meals, a few paid activities). Budget travel using hostels, casual food, and the streetcar can run closer to $50–$120 per day. Hotel rooms alone commonly run $120–$250 per night depending on season and neighborhood.
gettingAround: The French Quarter is compact and walkable — most sights are within a 15–20 minute walk of each other, so a car is optional if you're staying central. Streetcars connect the Quarter to the Garden District, Uptown, and City Park for $1.25 a ride, or a Jazzy Pass ($3/day, $8/3-day, $15/7-day) for unlimited rides. Rideshare and taxis fill the gaps for anything outside walking or streetcar range.

topAreas.name: French Quarter
topAreas.why: The most walkable base and the center of the action — music, food, and history within a compact grid. Expect noise and higher rates near Bourbon Street; quieter blocks are a short walk away.

topAreas.name: Garden District / Uptown
topAreas.why: Quieter, tree-lined, and historic, with easy streetcar access back into the Quarter. A good fit if you want distance from late-night noise without losing convenience.

topAreas.name: Warehouse District
topAreas.why: New Orleans' arts and museum hub, home to the National WWII Museum and a strong restaurant scene, a short walk or streetcar ride from the Quarter.

topAreas.name: Faubourg Marigny
topAreas.why: A quieter, more local alternative just past the Quarter, known for boutique guesthouses and a strong live-music strip on Frenchmen Street.

topThings.name: Jackson Square & Café du Monde
topThings.note: The classic first stop — beignets, street performers, and the square itself. Go early to beat both heat and crowds.

topThings.name: St. Charles Avenue streetcar ride
topThings.note: A cheap, scenic way to see the Garden District's historic mansions without booking a tour.

topThings.name: National WWII Museum
topThings.note: A large, well-regarded museum in the Warehouse District — plan a half day, not a quick stop.

topThings.name: French Quarter food or ghost tour
topThings.note: A guided tour is worth it for context on the city's history; book ahead for popular evening slots.

quickAnswers.q: What's the best time to visit New Orleans?
quickAnswers.a: October through early April for the best mix of weather, price, and crowd levels — avoid peak festival weekends if you want lower rates and easier reservations.

quickAnswers.q: Do I need a car in New Orleans?
quickAnswers.a: Not if you're staying in or near the French Quarter. Walking, the streetcar, and rideshare cover almost everything most visitors need.

quickAnswers.q: What should I budget per day?
quickAnswers.a: Plan on roughly $120–$270 per person per day for a mid-range trip, or $50–$120 for a tighter budget using hostels and casual food.
The French Quarter for walkability and nightlife, the Garden District or Uptown for a quieter base, or the Warehouse District if museums and restaurants are the priority.

quickAnswers.q: Is hurricane season a real risk for my trip?
quickAnswers.a: Hurricane season runs June–November, with August and September the most active. It doesn't rule out a trip, but build in travel-insurance and flexible-booking options if traveling in that window.
